name: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI)
aliases: herbal and dietary supplement liver injury

reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Injury is classified biochemically as hepatocellular (predominant ALT rise), cholestatic (predominant ALP rise) or mixed, using the R value derived from ALT and ALP relative to their upper limits of normal
Hy's law - a hepatocellular pattern with jaundice and no biliary obstruction - carries a high mortality and is a key marker of serious injury
Paracetamol causes dose-dependent (intrinsic) hepatotoxicity through the reactive metabolite NAPQI, whereas most other agents cause idiosyncratic, host-dependent injury
Co-amoxiclav and flucloxacillin are classic causes of a delayed cholestatic hepatitis that may begin after the course has finished
Always take a thorough drug history including over-the-counter agents, herbal and dietary supplements, and recreational drugs, as these are frequently overlooked culprits
Diagnosis is largely one of exclusion after viral, autoimmune, ischaemic and biliary causes have been ruled out; a temporal relationship and improvement on withdrawal support the diagnosis
The mainstay of management is prompt withdrawal of the suspected agent; N-acetylcysteine is the specific antidote for paracetamol DILI and is also used in some non-paracetamol acute liver failure
A rechallenge with the suspected drug is hazardous and generally avoided
reference.pathophysiology: Drug-induced liver injury arises either from intrinsic, dose-related toxicity or from idiosyncratic reactions that depend on host factors. In intrinsic injury, exemplified by paracetamol, saturation of normal conjugation pathways diverts metabolism to cytochrome P450, generating the reactive intermediate NAPQI which depletes glutathione and binds hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis. Idiosyncratic injury reflects unpredictable interactions between reactive metabolites, mitochondrial stress and adaptive immune responses, often with a genetic (including HLA) predisposition, and may be immunoallergic with fever, rash and eosinophilia. The biochemical picture reflects the target: hepatocellular necrosis raises transaminases, while injury to bile ducts or canalicular transport produces a cholestatic pattern with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin.
additionalDifferentials: Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, E) and other hepatotropic viruses
Alcohol-related and metabolic-associated fatty liver disease
Wilson disease and other inherited metabolic liver disorders
additionalInvestigations: Serial liver function tests with calculation of the R value to define pattern of injury
Coagulation profile (INR) and bilirubin as markers of synthetic dysfunction and severity
Viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune markers to exclude other causes
Abdominal ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging to exclude biliary obstruction
Paracetamol concentration and toxicology screen where overdose is possible
Liver biopsy in selected diagnostically uncertain or non-resolving cases
Eosinophil count where an immunoallergic mechanism is suspected
redFlags: Encephalopathy, coagulopathy or a rising INR indicating evolving acute liver failure
Jaundice with a hepatocellular pattern (Hy's law), predicting high mortality
Progressive rise in transaminases or bilirubin despite drug withdrawal
Features of a severe systemic hypersensitivity reaction such as DRESS
Hypoglycaemia, acidosis or renal impairment accompanying liver failure
reference.prognosis: Most idiosyncratic injury resolves after the offending drug is stopped, though cholestatic injury may take months to normalise. Development of jaundice in a hepatocellular pattern (Hy's law) predicts a substantial risk of death or need for transplantation, and fulminant failure carries a poor outcome without transplantation.
pitfalls: Overlooking herbal, dietary supplement or over-the-counter agents in the drug history
Attributing injury to a chronic medication while missing a recently introduced drug or a completed antibiotic course
Failing to recognise that cholestatic injury can begin after the culprit drug has been stopped
Delaying N-acetylcysteine in staggered or unclear-timing paracetamol exposure while awaiting levels
Rechallenging the patient with the suspected drug and precipitating severe recurrence
references: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Drug-induced liver injury
management: Identify and promptly withdraw the causative drug, including over-the-counter, herbal and recreational agents, and avoid rechallenge
Give the specific antidote N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol hepatotoxicity
Provide supportive care and monitor severity with serial liver enzymes, bilirubin and INR, watching for the poor prognosis of a jaundiced hepatocellular pattern (Hy's law)
Relieve cholestatic pruritus with agents such as colestyramine or ursodeoxycholic acid
Consider corticosteroids for immunoallergic or drug-induced autoimmune-type hepatitis and for hypersensitivity (DRESS) reactions
Refer urgently to a liver transplant centre when acute liver failure develops with coagulopathy or encephalopathy
Document the reaction, report it as a suspected adverse drug reaction and counsel the patient on avoidance
